# Finding an Edge {#sec-finding-an-edge}

Part III changes the question. Parts I and II were about what to do when the world cannot be
averaged. This part is about what to do when a genuine advantage exists: how to find it, how much
to stake on it, and how to survive the execution.

The first paper in the sequence is two pages long. Edward Thorp's "A Favorable Strategy for
Twenty-One" appeared in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, volume 47, issue 1,
pages 110 to 112, in January 1961 [@thorp1961]. OpenAlex records 29 citations for it.

Twenty-nine citations is a small number for a paper that changed an industry's operating rules and
started a line of research that runs to the present. The disparity is itself an argument: **some
results propagate through practice rather than through citation**, and a book that ranked
contributions by citation count would rank this paper last among the nine it covers.

## The structure that makes a casino game beatable

Casino games are usually designed so that each round is independent and the odds are fixed. Roulette
is the model: the wheel has no memory, the payouts are set by rule, and no sequence of observations
changes the expectation of the next spin.

Blackjack breaks the pattern in one specific way, and the whole paper turns on it.

**The cards are dealt from a finite deck without replacement.** After each hand, the deck that
remains is compositionally different from the deck that was shuffled, and the difference is
observable to anyone who has been paying attention.

That single fact converts the game from a sequence of identical independent trials into a
**state-dependent** process. The house edge is an average over states. Some states are better than
the average, some worse, and the expectation in a particular state depends on which cards remain.

The asymmetry that makes states matter is the rules themselves. The player acts first and may stop
at will; the dealer must draw according to a fixed schedule. When the remaining deck is rich in
ten-value cards, that asymmetry works in the player's favour, because a dealer required to draw into
a ten-heavy deck busts more often. When the deck is poor in them, the asymmetry works the other way.

Note the shape of the argument. No probability is estimated. The deck's composition is computed by
subtraction. **The edge is not forecast; it is read off a state.**

## Three kinds of advantage, and the one that fools people

The literature on this material conflates three distinct things, and the confusion survives into
present-day writing about trading.

| Kind | What it is | What it is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reduced disadvantage | Playing the basic strategy well, so the house edge is as small as the rules allow | An edge: the expectation is still negative |
| State edge | Some compositions of the remaining deck produce a positive expectation | A certainty: individual hands still lose |
| Outcome | Having won money | Evidence of an edge: it is also what variance looks like |

The third row is the one that costs money, and it costs money outside casinos more than inside them.

**Inside a casino the distinction is decidable.** The deck's composition is known, the payouts are
fixed, and the expectation in a state can be computed. A player who has won is not thereby a player
with an edge, and the arithmetic can prove it.

**Outside a casino it is not decidable, or not cheaply.** When the edge must be estimated rather
than computed, a winning record and a genuine edge look the same for a long time, which is why
sample-size questions that are trivial at a card table become the central practical problem in
investing. Part III returns to this in Chapter 24.

## What makes an edge usable

From the paper's structure, four requirements, and they are worth stating because each is routinely
missing in domains where people claim edges.

**Observability.** The state must be readable. Card composition is readable by counting. Many
market states are not readable, or are readable only with a delay that removes the advantage.

**Computability.** The state must translate into an expectation by a rule the practitioner can
apply. The paper's contribution is partly the counting scheme — a reduction of the deck to one or
two numbers a person can hold in mind.

**Stationarity of the rule.** The relationship between state and expectation must hold while you
are using it. It did, until the casinos changed the rules.

**Exposure to the favourable states.** The edge is realised only if the stake is larger in the good
states than in the bad ones. **Finding the edge is the first half; Chapter 20 handles the second.**

## From the card table to the market

The migration of this mathematics into finance is not a metaphor. The same author made it, and the
same structure appears on both sides.

**In both cases there is a state, and the expectation depends on it.** In the casino the state is
the deck; in a market it might be a spread, a volatility level, a funding condition, or a
positioning imbalance.

**In both cases the practitioner's job is to read the state and size the stake accordingly.**

The difference is decisive, and it is the reason Part III is harder than Parts I and II.

**At a card table the edge is computed. In a market it is estimated.** Computation has an error of
zero — the arithmetic is the truth about the deck — while estimation has an error that is not merely
nonzero but hard to quantify, for all the reasons Part I assembled.

That difference propagates into everything downstream. A computed edge supports an optimal stake
computed to the decimal. An estimated edge supports a stake you can defend, which is a weaker object
and the reason Chapter 21 exists.

## Grading it

In the vocabulary of Chapter 26.

**The structural claim is grade I.** That a state-dependent game with an observable state and a
computable expectation contains favourable states is arithmetic, and it does not depend on any
estimate.

**Its practical form is grade II.** That a particular game is beatable in practice depends on rules,
enforcement, and costs. The casino version did not survive its regime change: when the operating
rules were altered, the advantage shrank.

**The transfer to other domains is grade III, and it is where the paper is most often over-read.**
"States with favourable expectations exist everywhere" is a statement about the structure of
stochastic processes and is true almost by definition. "You can find them in any given market" is
an empirical claim that requires the four requirements above, and they are not usually met.

## Claim and tool

The claim: that a game with a finite deck and a fixed dealer rule has states in which the player's
expectation is positive, and that the states are identifiable in real time.

The tool: the state-dependence argument itself, and the discipline of separating an edge from a
result. **The tool is what transferred; the specific counting schemes did not.**

## Boundary conditions

The result requires an observable state, a stable rule linking state to expectation, and a stake
that can be varied. Remove any of the three and the advantage cannot be realised even if it exists.

It fails where the rule is changed in response to its discovery, which is what happened and which
recurs in every domain where a structural advantage becomes visible.

And it says nothing about size. A positive expectation with the wrong stake produces ruin, which is
the subject of the next chapter.

## Where state dependence appears outside a casino

The structural feature that made blackjack beatable is not unique to cards, and identifying it
elsewhere is the transferable part of the paper.

**The feature, restated.** An observable state influences the expectation of the next outcome, and the
state is not fully priced.

**Four instances, with the requirement they fail or satisfy.**

**Order flow and inventory.** A dealer who must quote regardless of inventory has a state — the
position — that shifts the price at which they will trade. The state is observable in the quotes. What
fails is stationarity: the relationship is well known to the participants, and its value depends on who
else is present.

**Funding conditions.** The price of borrowing a security moves with scarcity, and scarcity is
observable before the price adjusts. Computable, stable over months, and crowded almost immediately.
**This is the pattern of an edge whose life is short.**

**Volatility regimes.** Where the scale of fluctuations clusters, the state is partly observable and
persistent. What fails is the requirement of a computable expectation: the state predicts dispersion,
which is not a payoff.

**Seasonal and calendar structure.** An observable state with a documented effect, whose failure mode
is that it has been documented. **Publication is the erosion mechanism.**

**What the four have in common.** Each satisfies some of the four requirements and fails others, and
the requirement most often failed is stability — not of the statistics, but of the rule linking state
to expectation. **That is the requirement that makes a structural source valuable, which is the
argument Chapter 25 develops at length.**

## An edge that would not survive the four requirements

A negative example is worth as much as the positive one, and the fastest way to apply the framework is
to test candidate edges against the four requirements in order.

Take a claim of the form: this asset class outperforms after a particular policy announcement.

**Observability.** The state is public at the announcement. Satisfied, and satisfied for everyone at
once, which is already a problem for the second requirement.

**Computability.** The expected excess return cannot be computed from the announcement; it is
estimated from the history of previous announcements. This is the transition from the casino to the
market, and it is where most candidate edges fail: the edge is inferred rather than read off.

**Stationarity.** Policy regimes change, and the sample of previous announcements is small. The rule
linking announcement to return is itself an estimated object with a decay rate that cannot be
measured from the sample that generated it.

**Exposure to favourable states.** Requires knowing which states are favourable, which requires the
second and third requirements.

**The verdict.** One requirement satisfied, three failed, and the failure of the second is decisive:
the edge is estimated, so everything in Part III's sizing machinery applies with its discount, and
everything in Chapter 24's sampling arithmetic applies to the evidence. **An edge that fails the
computability requirement is not thereby unusable. It is an edge that has to be sized with a large
discount and treated as one of many candidates rather than as a discovery.**

## The edge checklist in one page

Chapter 18's four requirements and Part III's machinery reduce to a page. A practitioner evaluating a
candidate edge runs it in this order, because the early questions are cheap and each can end the
exercise.

**One. Is the state observable, in real time, by me?** If the state is visible only after the fact, the
edge cannot be used whatever its statistical properties.

**Two. Is the expectation computable from the state, or must it be estimated?** This is the decisive
question. **Computed means the casino case: exact arithmetic, no discount. Estimated means everything in
Parts I and III applies, including the sampling arithmetic of Chapter 24.**

**Three. How long will the rule linking state to expectation hold?** Mechanism stability, institutional
stability, statistical evidence. **Where none is available, the answer is "unknown" and the edge is a
candidate rather than a position.**

**Four. What is the capacity?** An order of magnitude is enough. **A strategy whose capacity is smaller
than the capital available to it is a component, not a strategy.**

**Five. What is the annual cost, and what fraction of the capital can pay it?** Where the cost cannot be
funded from a source independent of the edge, the position will be abandoned at the wrong moment.

**Six. What is the discount, and what coefficient of variation justifies it?** Writing the number is the
step that most often ends the analysis, which is the point of requiring it.

**Seven. What is the exit condition, set in advance?** A rule, a date, or a threshold. **Without one, the
decision to stop will be made monthly by the person with the strongest interest in continuing.**

**What the checklist is not.** It is not a scoring system. A candidate that fails question two can still
be worth running at a size that assumes the estimate is wrong. **What it does is force the failure to be
stated rather than discovered.**

## The edge that is real but unactionable

Between edges that work and edges that do not, there is a category that causes more institutional difficulty
than either: edges that exist and cannot be used.

**The sources of unactionability. Four.**

**Observability with a delay.** The state is identifiable only after the position would have to be taken.

**Size below the minimum.** The edge exists at a scale smaller than the smallest position the institution can
hold, after costs and minimum ticket sizes. **A strategy returning two percent annually on a million dollars
is not a strategy for a fund with a hundred million to deploy.**

**Operational impossibility.** The edge requires a capability the institution does not have: intraday
execution, a short borrow, a legal structure, a licence.

**Constraint conflict.** The edge requires a position the institution's mandate forbids, or requires
concentration that its risk limits prohibit.

**Why this category is difficult.** Because the edge is real, the analysis is correct, and the conclusion is
that nothing can be done. **An organisation that evaluates research by the quality of its findings will
reward the analysis and have nothing to show for it, which produces pressure to overlook the
unactionability.**

**What to record.** For each candidate, the constraint that binds, and whether it is structural or
institutional. **Institutional constraints can be changed by a decision; structural ones cannot. Confusing
the two is how organisations spend years on research they cannot deploy.**

**What to do with a portfolio of unactionable edges.** Keep them. **A constraint that binds now may not bind
later, and an edge documented at the time it was found is a cheaper asset than one that must be rediscovered
under time pressure. This is the pipeline argument of Chapter 25, applied to a category of candidate that
usually gets discarded.**

## The edge versus the strategy

A candidate edge and a tradeable strategy are different objects, and the gap between them is where most
research time is lost.

**The edge. A claim about a state.** The expectation of an outcome differs from the market's implied
expectation under specified conditions.

**The strategy. The edge plus five decisions.** Position sizing, entry and exit rules, execution venue,
holding period, and risk limits.

**Why they are confused.** Because an edge presented in isolation looks like a strategy. **The five decisions
determine whether the edge is realised, and none of them is implied by the edge.**

**Three cases where the gap is large.**

**An edge that requires a size the market cannot absorb.** The capacity problem, arriving before any
execution work is done.

**An edge whose exit rule determines the outcome.** A mispricing that converges in a year and a funding
constraint of three months are incompatible, and the incompatibility is a property of the strategy.

**An edge requiring a holding period longer than the evidence base.** The edge is measured over one regime
and requires a position lasting through another.

**What to record when an edge is found.** The edge, the five decisions with their justifications, and the
constraint that binds. **A one-page note per candidate, and the discipline converts a research finding into a
deployable object or exposes the constraint early.**

**Why this matters for the checklist.** The four requirements of this chapter establish that an edge exists.
**They do not establish that a strategy exists, and the checklist's later questions — capacity, cost, exit —
are the ones that close the gap.**

## What a favourable state is not

The paper's contribution is a state whose expectation is positive. The term is used loosely in the material
that followed, and the four common misreadings are worth naming.

**Not an unlikely event.** A favourable state is one where the expectation is positive, which says nothing
about the probability of winning the next round. **A state can be favourable and the next hand can lose,
and both statements are consistent.**

**Not an edge in the market's sense.** A favourable state is a property of the game's structure. **An edge
in a market requires the state to be observable, the expectation to be computable or estimable, and the
rules to persist — the four requirements the chapter sets out.**

**Not a prediction.** The state is read from the current configuration rather than forecast. **A player who
predicts the state rather than reading it has replaced a computation with an estimate, which is the
transition the chapter's later sections describe.**

**Not a licence to bet the maximum.** A favourable state means positive expectation, and positive
expectation with the wrong stake produces ruin. **The sizing rules of Part III apply to a favourable state
exactly as they apply to an estimated edge, with the discount determined by whether the expectation was
computed or estimated.**

**Why the misreadings matter. One reason.** Each of them converts a statement about the structure of a game
into a statement about the future, and the conversion is the same error in four forms. **The paper's claim is
narrow: a state, an expectation, a rule. Widening it is what produces the confident and wrong uses.**

**What to check in a claimed favourable state. Three questions.**

**Is the state observable now?** Not predicted, observed.

**Is the expectation computed or estimated?** Which determines the discount and the evidential status.

**What ends the state?** A deck, a rule, a market structure. **A state without an ending condition is a
strategy without a duration, and the chapter on decay applies.**

A closing summary. Read the state. Not forecast it. Compute if possible. Estimate if not. Discount either way. Check capacity first. Cap the size. Set the exit. Review the mechanism.

## The four requirements as a screening interview

The four requirements are stated as an analytical checklist. They also function as a list of questions for
someone presenting an edge, and the interview form is worth having.

**Observability. One question.** What does the state look like, and when can you see it. **Which asks for an
operational description rather than a definition.**

**Computability. One question.** How is the expectation obtained from the state. **An arithmetic answer
indicates a computed edge; a historical answer indicates an estimated one, and the two carry different
discounts.**

**Stationarity. One question.** What has to stay the same for the rule to keep working, and what would tell you
it had not. **Which asks for the monitor as well as the assumption.**

**Exposure to favourable states. One question.** How does the size vary with the state, and who decides that.
**Which asks whether the edge is connected to the position.**

**What the interview establishes. Two things.**

**Whether the edge exists as a description.** Oddly, this is not the primary output. **Most candidates fail the
second or third question rather than the first.**

**Whether the presenter has thought about duration.** Which is the question that separates a research finding
from a deployable strategy.

**What the interview does not establish. The edge itself.** The four questions are about structure. **An edge
that passes all four may still be worthless, and one that fails the third may be worth running at a size that
assumes it will die.**

**Why the interview form is worth stating.** Because a checklist is filled in by one person and an interview
produces answers that can be recorded. **Four questions, four recorded answers, and the record is what makes
the edge's evaluation revisitable when the monitor fires.**

**What to do when an answer is missing.** Record it as missing. **The missing answer is the finding, and it is
more useful than an answer supplied under pressure.**

## The four requirements and the transition to Part III

The four requirements establish that an edge exists. The next chapters assume one does, and the transition
between them is where the requirements do their work for the sizing argument.

**What the requirements determine. One thing.** Whether the expectation is computed or estimated. **Computed
means the casino case; estimated means everything in Parts I and III applies, including the sampling arithmetic
and the discount.**

**What follows for the sizing rule. Two branches.**

**Computed. The parameters are known.** The fraction is arithmetic and the discount's coefficient of variation
is small. **Which is the case the criterion was designed for.**

**Estimated. The parameters are uncertain.** The fraction is discounted, the drawdown is checked against
tolerance, and the sampling arithmetic determines what evidence would justify a larger commitment. **Which is
the case the rest of the book addresses.**

**What the transition requires of a reader. One judgement.** Which branch applies. **A reader who treats an
estimated edge as computed will size it too large; one who treats a computed edge as estimated will size it
too small and will distrust a rule that is exact.**

**Why the four requirements are placed before the sizing chapters.** Because they determine the branch. **An
edge's observability, computability, persistence and exposure are the inputs to the question "computed or
estimated", and the question is what the rest of Part III answers.**

**What happens when the branch is unclear. One rule.** Treat it as estimated. **The cost is a smaller position
and a discount that turns out to have been unnecessary, and the alternative cost is a position sized on an
assumption that was not tested.**

**What the chapter leaves for the next one.** The stake. **The requirements establish that an edge exists and
how well it is known; the currency of the next chapters is how much of the capital it justifies.**

## The edge and the three documents it needs

An edge that is going to be funded needs three documents, and their absence is what turns a research finding
into an unmanaged position.

**One. A statement of the state.** What is observed, how it is observed, and when. **Which is the observability
requirement, written down, and it is what makes the monitor possible.**

**Two. A statement of the connection.** How the expectation is obtained from the state, whether computed or
estimated, and with what uncertainty. **Which is the computability requirement and it determines the discount.**

**Three. A statement of the ending.** What has to stay the same, what would signal that it had not, and the exit
condition. **Which covers the persistence requirement and the pre-committed exit together, and it is the document
most often missing.**

**What the three documents produce. One thing.** A strategy rather than an edge. **The five decisions of the
chapter's later section — sizing, entry and exit, venue, holding period, limits — are each informed by one of the
three.**

**What their absence produces. Two failures.**

**A position with no monitor.** Which is a position held until its returns become obviously bad.

**A position with no exit condition.** Which is a position held past the point where its justification expired.

**Why three documents rather than a memorandum.** Because each answers a question that arises at a different
moment: the state at the monitor, the connection at the sizing decision, the ending at the review. **Three
one-page notes, each used at its own occasion.**

**What a funder should ask for. The third document.** Because the first two are what the presenter has thought
about and the third is what they have not. **The absence of an ending is the finding, and asking for it is the
cheapest available test of whether the edge has been considered as a position.**

## The edge and three questions about its size

The chapter establishes whether an edge exists. Three questions about size determine whether it can be used, and
they are asked in this order.

**How large is the position the edge supports.** Which follows from the expectation and its uncertainty, and
requires the sizing machinery of Part III. **The answer is a fraction with a discount, or a bound.**

**How large is the position the market will absorb.** Which is the capacity question and comes before the
sizing one in practice, because a fraction of capital that exceeds capacity is not available. **The answer is an
order of magnitude.**

**How large is the position the firm can fund through its drawdown.** Which is the holder's constraint and is
usually the binding one. **The answer is a number derived from the sources of capital that do not depend on the
strategy.**

**Which of the three binds. Usually the smallest.** Which is why the order matters: computing the sizing
fraction first produces a number that the other two constraints then overrule.

**What the three questions have in common. One input each.** The first needs an estimate and its uncertainty, the
second needs market structure, and the third needs the firm's balance sheet. **Three different bodies of
information for one decision.**

**How to use the three in a decision. One line per question.** Which produces a position size and a record of
which constraint bound it. **The record is what makes the next decision faster, because the binding constraint is
usually the same across a firm's strategies.**

**Why the three belong with the edge's evaluation.** Because an edge that cannot be sized within all three is not
deployable at the size the analysis implies. **Three questions, three inputs, and the smallest answer is the
position.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The paper's text was not available to me. The argument above follows its title, abstract, citation
record, and the account given in the author's own later writing; no counting scheme, threshold, or
numerical result from the paper is reproduced here, and the description of the basic strategy is
presented without citing a specific source because I could not verify the reference I had in mind.

The claim that casino rules were altered in response to the work is well documented as a sequence of
events; the chapter uses it as an example of a regime change rather than as a factual finding about
any particular establishment.
